title: Cap. VIII Arg. 9 (Thomas of Argentina): adult reprobation from foresight of final bad use of free will
latin: Ex antiquis Scholasticis Thomas de Argentina fatetur se communem opinionem Theologorum deserere, ac conatur contra eos hanc conclusionem probare, Causam reprobationis quoad adultos esse malum usum liberi arbitrii, usque ad finem vitae in ipsis duraturum, ab aeterno a Deo praescitum. Quae opinio verbis, non sensu, differt a Jesuitica et Arminiana. Audiamus igitur Argentinae rationes.
pass_a: From the ancient Scholastics Thomas of Argentina confesses that he deserts the common opinion of the Theologians, and tries against them to prove this conclusion, That the cause of reprobation as to adults is the evil use of free will, about to last in them unto the end of life, foresighted from eternity by God. Which opinion differs in words, not in sense, from the Jesuit and Arminian. Let us therefore hear the reasons of Argentina.
pass_b: Among the older Scholastics, Thomas of Argentina admits he deserts the common opinion of the theologians, and tries against them to prove this: that the cause of reprobation as to adults is the evil use of free will lasting in them to life's end, foresighted by God from eternity. That opinion differs in words, not in sense, from the Jesuit and Arminian. Let us hear Argentina's reasons.

foresighted final bad use as cause

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 9: syllogism — no one ordained to eternal punishment without precognition of cause
latin: Ad poenam aeternam, inquit, nullus ordinatur a justo Judice sine praecognitione causae. Sed omnis reprobatus est ad poenam a Deo justo Judice deputatus: Ergo non nisi ex praeviso malo usu liberi arbitrii ad finem usque duraturo. Quod idem est ac si dixisset cum Jesuitis et Arminianis, non nisi ex praevisa infidelitate et inobedientia.
pass_a: Unto eternal punishment, says he, no one is ordained by a just Judge without precognition of the cause. But every reprobate is deputed unto punishment by God the just Judge: Therefore not except from the foresighted evil use of free will about to last unto the end. Which is the same as if he had said with the Jesuits and Arminians, not except from foresighted unbelief and disobedience.
pass_b: To eternal punishment, he says, no one is ordained by a just Judge without precognition of the cause. But every reprobate is deputed to punishment by God the just Judge. Therefore only from foresighted evil use of free will lasting to the end — which is the same as saying with Jesuits and Arminians: only from foresighted unbelief and disobedience.

lemmas.gloss: just Judge needs precognition of cause

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 9 Resp.: reprobation is denial of unowed benefit, not adjudication to punishment
latin: Respondeo, nos per reprobationem intelligere illam Divinae providentiae partem secundum quam Deus vult quibusdam negare specialem gratiam, ac permittere ut deficiant a fine beatitudinis; sicut per praedestinationem intelligimus illam alteram partem Divinae providentiae secundum quam voluit quibusdam praeparare ac donare hanc gratiam specialem, eosdemque ad gloriam ac beatitudinem infallibiliter perducere. Hoc posito, negamus reprobationem hanc esse deputationem vel adjudicationem ad poenam. Est quidem beneficii indebiti ex sola Dei voluntate libera denegatio: sed non est supplicii indebiti ex sola Dei voluntate imperiosa inflictio. Sequitur quidem in omnibus reprobis ordinatio ad poenam, et poenae impositio; atque haec utraque recte dicuntur respicere personae sic ordinatae et puniendae finalem permansionem in peccato: sed in ipso formali actu reprobationis ordinatio personae reprobatae ad mortem aeternam nondum continetur. Fallere igitur nos conantur hujusmodi argumentationibus, dum quae eidem subjecto competunt, ex iisdem causis falso nasci praesumunt; quasi necesse esset, quia omnis reprobatus est etiam ad poenam ordinatus, ideo hanc reprobationem atque hanc ad poenam ordinationem ex iisdem causis dependere. Nos autem defendimus, utcunque iidem homines, qui sunt reprobati, semper etiam sint ad poenam deputati, tamen hanc reprobationem ex sola libertate voluntatis Divinae manasse, ordinationem autem ad poenam ex praeviso eorundem peccato originem traxisse.
pass_a: I answer that we understand by reprobation that part of Divine providence according to which God wills to deny to certain ones special grace, and to permit that they fall short of the end of beatitude; as by predestination we understand that other part of Divine providence according to which he willed to prepare and give to certain ones this special grace, and infallibly to lead the same unto glory and beatitude. This being posited, we deny that this reprobation is a deputation or adjudication unto punishment. It is indeed the free denial of an unowed benefit from the will of God alone: but it is not the imperious infliction of an unowed punishment from the will of God alone. There does indeed follow in all the reprobate an ordination unto punishment, and the imposition of punishment; and these both are rightly said to regard the final remaining in sin of the person so ordained and to be punished: but in the very formal act of reprobation the ordination of the reprobated person unto eternal death is not yet contained. They therefore try to deceive us with argumentations of this kind, while they falsely presume that things which compete to the same subject are born from the same causes; as if it were necessary, because every reprobate is also ordained unto punishment, that therefore this reprobation and this ordination unto punishment depend from the same causes. But we defend that, howsoever the same men who are reprobated are always also deputed unto punishment, yet this reprobation flowed from the sole liberty of the Divine will, but the ordination unto punishment drew origin from their foresighted sin.
pass_b: I answer: by reprobation we mean that part of divine providence by which God wills to deny certain ones special grace and permit them to fall short of beatitude's end — as by predestination we mean that other part by which he willed to prepare and give certain ones that special grace and lead them infallibly to glory and beatitude. On that footing, we deny that this reprobation is a deputation or adjudication to punishment. It is free denial of an unowed benefit from God's will alone; it is not imperious infliction of an unowed penalty from God's will alone. Yes, in all the reprobate there follows ordination to punishment and imposition of punishment — and both rightly regard that person's final remaining in sin. But in the formal act of reprobation itself, ordination of the reprobate person to eternal death is not yet contained. Such arguments try to deceive us by presuming that what belongs to the same subject must spring from the same causes — as if, because every reprobate is also ordained to punishment, reprobation and that ordination to punishment must depend on the same causes. We hold: however much the same men who are reprobated are always also deputed to punishment, this reprobation flowed from the sole liberty of the divine will, while ordination to punishment drew its origin from their foresighted sin.

lemmas.gloss: same subject ≠ same cause for reprobation and penalty

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 10: God as spiritual sun — reprobation from foresight of putting an obstacle to grace
latin: Deus est quasi Sol quidam radios gratiae spiritualis ubique diffundens: Ergo quantum in se est, gratiam spiritualem omnibus impertit, nisi diffusis gratiae suae radiis obicem ponant. Quod igitur quosdam gratiae expertes relinquit et reprobat, id inde evenit, quod praevidit hosce ut obicem ponentes gratiae suae. Reprobatio igitur est ex praeviso hoc malo usu liberi arbitrii.
pass_a: God is as it were a certain Sun everywhere diffusing the rays of spiritual grace: Therefore as much as in him is, he imparts spiritual grace unto all, unless they put an obstacle to the diffused rays of his grace. That therefore he leaves certain ones void of grace and reprobates them, happens thence, that he foresaw these as putting an obstacle to his grace. Reprobation therefore is from this foresighted evil use of free will.
pass_b: Tenth: God is as it were a Sun everywhere diffusing rays of spiritual grace. Therefore, as much as in him lies, he imparts spiritual grace to all, unless they put an obstacle to those diffused rays. That he leaves some void of grace and reprobates them happens because he foresaw them putting an obstacle to his grace. So reprobation is from that foresighted evil use of free will.

lemmas.gloss: sun analogy for universal grace diffusion
foresight of obstacle as cause of reprobation

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 10 Resp.: sun not by natural necessity; special ray of mercy not offered to all alike
latin: In multis deficit haec comparatio. Primo, licet Deus haud incommode dicatur Sol spiritualis, tamen non diffundit radios suos naturali necessitate, sed dispensatione voluntaria. Ergo quantum in se non ad omnes aequaliter et uniformiter eos diffundit. Secundo, ut largiamur Deum quosdam communes gratiae radios ad omnes et singulos diffundere (quae de re nunc non litigabimus), tamen specialem hunc et eximium radium specialis misericordiae, quantum in se est, omnibus et singulis promiscue eum praebere, nunquam concedemus.
pass_a: In many things this comparison fails. First, although God is not inconveniently called a spiritual Sun, yet he does not diffuse his rays by natural necessity, but by voluntary dispensation. Therefore as much as in him he does not diffuse them unto all equally and uniformly. Secondly, though we grant that God diffuses certain common rays of grace unto all and singular (about which matter we will not now litigate), yet that he, as much as in him is, promiscuously offers this special and excellent ray of special mercy unto all and singular, we will never concede.
pass_b: The comparison fails in many ways. First: though God is not badly called a spiritual Sun, he does not diffuse his rays by natural necessity but by voluntary dispensation. So as much as in him lies, he does not diffuse them to all equally and uniformly. Second: even if we grant that God diffuses certain common rays of grace to each and all (we will not litigate that now), we will never concede that, as much as in him lies, he promiscuously offers this special excellent ray of special mercy to each and all.

lemmas.gloss: grace rays not by natural necessity
special mercy ray not offered to all alike

title: Cap. VIII Arg. 10 Resp.: if from foresight of obstacles, all would be reprobate; election softens some (Aquinas)
latin: Tertio, ubi Deus praesumitur nemini velle denegare hanc specialem misericordiam, quae electionis propria est, atque idcirco neminem reprobare, nisi qui praevisus fuerit ut gratiae Divinae obicem injiciens perverso usu liberi sui arbitrii, non animadvertit Argentina, hanc exceptionem de obice opponendo ad omnes et singulos pertinere in statu peccati consideratos. Nam prudenter observatum est ab Aquinate: Id quod dici solet, IN POTESTATE LIBERI ARBITRII ESSE NE IMPEDIMENTUM GRATIAE PRAESTET, de iis vere dicitur in quibus naturalis potentia integra fuerit: Quod per inordinationem praecedentem declinaverit ad malum, jam non erit omnino in sua potestate ut velit impedimentum praestare. Contr. Gent. lib. 3. cap. 160. Cum igitur omnes mortales ex se parati sint ad obices ponendos, et de facto ponant quamplurimos, si Deus ex tali praevisione reprobaret, omnes quotquot sumus, ne uno quidem excepto, reprobasset. Praedestinationis ergo et reprobationis specimen in hoc elucet, quod cum obices ponantur ab omnibus, Deus, ex abundantia misericordiae suae, quosdam impedimentis suis, tamen efficacibus et miris modis tandem emollire, et ad fidem et resipiscentiam convertere decrevit; alios autem eodem in modo gratiae suae obluctantes non emollire decrevit, sed in duritia sua et pervicacia obduratos relinquere. Denique quod ex praemissis infertur, nempe Deum ab aeterno praevidisse quosdam ut finaliter bene usuros libero arbitrio, alios ut finaliter male usuros eodem, atque ita decreto hanc praevisionem subsequente hos elegisse, illos reprobasse, id nullo modo potest consistere. Bonus enim et sanus usus liberi arbitrii in finem usque perseverans non nisi ex gratia electionis dimanavit; ergo electionem antecedentem praesupponit: E contra, malus usus liberi arbitrii, perdurans ad extremum usque halitum, non praevidetur nisi praesupposita in Deo voluntate negandi illam specialem gratiam, cui nullum cor, quantumvis durum, resistit: At haec voluntas Dei est voluntas reprobandi: Praevisio igitur cordis finaliter obdurati est quiddam reprobatione posterius, atque idcirco ratio sive causa reprobationis inde peti non potest.
pass_a: Thirdly, where God is presumed to will to deny to no one this special mercy which is proper to election, and therefore to reprobate no one except who shall have been foresighted as casting an obstacle to Divine grace by the perverse use of his free will, Argentina does not notice that this exception concerning opposing an obstacle pertains unto all and singular considered in the state of sin. For it was prudently observed by Aquinas: That which is wont to be said, THAT IT IS IN THE POWER OF FREE WILL NOT TO PRESENT AN IMPEDIMENT TO GRACE, is truly said of those in whom natural power shall have been intact: He who by preceding inordination has declined unto evil, will not now be altogether in his power that he will to present an impediment. Against the Gentiles book 3, chapter 160. Since therefore all mortals of themselves are ready unto putting obstacles, and in fact put very many, if God were to reprobate from such foresight, he would have reprobated all whosoever we are, not even one excepted. The specimen therefore of predestination and of reprobation shines forth in this, that although obstacles are put by all, God, from the abundance of his mercy, decreed finally to soften certain ones from their impediments, yet by efficacious and wondrous ways, and to convert them unto faith and repentance; but others struggling in the same manner against his grace he decreed not to soften, but to leave hardened in their hardness and obstinacy. Finally what is inferred from the premises, namely that God from eternity foresaw certain ones as finally about to use free will well, others as finally about to use the same ill, and so by a decree following this foresight elected these, reprobated those, that can by no means stand. For the good and sound use of free will persevering unto the end flowed not except from the grace of election; therefore it presupposes antecedent election: On the contrary, the evil use of free will, lasting unto the last breath, is not foresighted unless the will in God of denying that special grace, which no heart howsoever hard resists, be presupposed: But this will of God is the will of reprobating: Foresight therefore of a heart finally hardened is something later than reprobation, and therefore the reason or cause of reprobation cannot be sought thence.
pass_b: Third: where God is presumed to will to deny no one that special mercy proper to election, and so to reprobate no one except who is foresighted as casting an obstacle to divine grace by perverse use of free will, Argentina misses that this exception about opposing an obstacle applies to each and all considered in the state of sin. Aquinas observed prudently (Contra Gentiles 3.160): the saying IT IS IN THE POWER OF FREE WILL NOT TO PRESENT AN IMPEDIMENT TO GRACE is truly said of those whose natural power is intact; he who by prior inordination has declined to evil is no longer altogether in his power so to will as to present an impediment. Since all mortals are of themselves ready to put obstacles, and in fact put very many, if God reprobated from such foresight he would have reprobated every one of us, not one excepted. So the pattern of predestination and reprobation shines here: though all put obstacles, God from abundance of mercy decreed finally to soften some — by efficacious and wondrous ways — out of their impediments and convert them to faith and repentance; others struggling the same way against his grace he decreed not to soften, but to leave hardened in their hardness and obstinacy. Finally the inference — that God from eternity foresaw some as finally using free will well, others ill, and by a decree following that foresight elected these and reprobated those — cannot stand. Good sound use of free will persevering to the end flowed only from election's grace, so it presupposes antecedent election. Conversely, evil use lasting to the last breath is not foresighted unless God's will to deny that special grace — which no heart, however hard, resists — is presupposed. That will of God is the will to reprobate. So foresight of a finally hardened heart is something later than reprobation; the reason or cause of reprobation cannot be sought from it.

lemmas.gloss: fallen will not intact against grace impediment
foresight of final hardness later than reprobation
